screens.title: Semi‑Synchronous Replication and GTID
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we examine a practical gap in MySQL replication: the data loss window that can occur with asynchronous replication, and two techniques DBAs use to close that gap. First, we’ll define semi‑synchronous replication — a middle ground where the source waits for a receipt from at least one replica so committed transactions are at least received by another server. You’ll see how that acknowledgement changes durability guarantees and what it does not guarantee, namely immediate application on the replica. Second, we’ll introduce Global Transaction Identifiers, or GTIDs, which convert replication from file/position based tracking to transaction‑based tracking. I’ll show how GTIDs simplify failover and provisioning and which server settings are required. Throughout the lesson you’ll walk through the exact commands used to install and enable semi‑sync plugins on a source and a replica, the my. cnf fragments needed for persistence, and the verification commands such as SHOW STATUS and SHOW MASTER STATUS. By the end you will understand how semi‑sync reduces data loss risk, how GTIDs make failover deterministic, and what common configuration mistakes to avoid when enabling these features.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Semi‑synchronous replication reduces the chance of committed transactions being lost by waiting for receipt acknowledgement; GTIDs convert replication to transaction-based operations to simplify failover and provisioning.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Semi‑Sync & GTID
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Semi‑Synchronous Replication and GTID

What you will learn: how to enable semi‑sync, what the acknowledgement means, how to set up GTID mode, and what to monitor.

Why this matters
Reducing the chance of committed transaction loss and making failover predictable are essential for production DBAs.
What you will do
Walk through plugin installation commands, configuration files and commands to verify semi‑sync and GTID status.
In this lesson
Data‑loss window, semi‑sync mechanism, plugin setup, monitoring.
Coming up
GTID format and enabling gtid_mode safely.
Hands-on
Terminal walkthrough of INSTALL PLUGIN and SHOW STATUS commands.
Concept Map
S
Source server
R
Replica (semi‑sync client)
The source waits for a receipt from a semi‑sync replica, then responds success to the client; if timeout occurs, the source falls back to asynchronous behavior.
Quick commands
-- On source:
INSTALL PLUGIN rpl_semi_sync_source SONAME 'mysql_semi_sync_source.so';
SET GLOBAL rpl_semi_sync_source_enabled = ON;
SET GLOBAL rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout = 5000;

-- On replica:
INSTALL PLUGIN rpl_semi_sync_replica SONAME 'mysql_semi_sync_replica.so';
SET GLOBAL rpl_semi_sync_replica_enabled = ON;

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These four objectives map to practical DBA actions and conceptual understanding you need for robust replication. First, you will explain why asynchronous replication can lose committed transactions if the source fails before the binlog event reaches any replica. A concrete example is a high‑traffic write just committed on the primary that is still buffered for network transfer. Second, you will describe how semi‑synchronous replication reduces that risk by requiring a replica receipt before the source returns success, and you will explain the difference between receipt and application on the replica. Third, you will configure semi‑synchronous plugins on both source and replica, set rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout appropriately, and persist those settings in my. cnf so they survive restarts. Finally, you will define GTIDs, enable gtid_mode with enforce_gtid_consistency, and verify GTID status using SHOW MASTER STATUS and SHOW REPLICA STATUS. Each objective connects concept and command so you can both reason about durability and execute configuration in a controlled, testable way.

Interpretation cards
Fallbacks

Connected clients

screens.title: The data‑loss window in asynchronous replication
screens.narratorSegment: Asynchronous replication trades immediate durability for low commit latency by not waiting for any replica confirmation before returning success to a client. To be precise: when the source commits a transaction and writes the event to its binary log, it hands off the event to the network and immediately returns success. If the source crashes before that event is received or written by any replica, the transaction is effectively lost — it exists in the source binary log or memory but not on any surviving server. A concrete example is a busy write-heavy system where a commit occurs and the network to the replicas is partitioned for a few seconds; if the primary fails during that partition, those last commits vanish. This is important because many production SLAs require zero or near-zero data loss. A common misconception is to equate 'committed' with 'durable across servers' in asynchronous setups. The correct mental model is that commit on the source guarantees local durability only. The takeaway is that understanding this window is the motivation for semi‑synchronous replication: we need a middle ground that reduces the chance of losing committed work while keeping latency acceptable. Reflect: in your environment, which transactions absolutely cannot be lost and are worth the extra latency to protect?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Asynchronous commit returns success before any replica receives the binlog event, creating a data loss window if the source fails.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Data‑loss window
Definition and example

Asynchronous replication returns commit success without waiting for replica receipt. If the source fails before the event reaches any replica, the transaction can be lost.

  • Example: a last-second write is committed and the network partitions; the primary crashes before any replica stores the event.
  • Misconception: "Commit means replicated" — not true for async replication.
  • Impact: SLAs that require no data loss must consider replication mode.
Why it matters

Knowing the data loss window informs whether you need semi‑sync or a different HA strategy for critical writes.

Terminal illustration
-- Client issues a write and sees success immediately
COMMIT; -- returns OK on primary
-- Meanwhile, the binlog event is in transit; if primary crashes now, replicas may not have it.
Analogy: Dropping a package from a truck before it reaches a safe mailbox.

screens.title: How semi‑synchronous replication works
screens.narratorSegment: Semi‑synchronous replication offers a compromise: the source waits for at least one configured replica to acknowledge receipt of the binary log event before returning success to the client. Concretely, the sequence is: the source commits and writes the event to its binary log, sends the event to connected replicas, and waits for a receipt acknowledgement from one semi‑sync replica. If an acknowledgement arrives within rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout, the source returns success; if no acknowledgement arrives within the timeout, the source falls back to asynchronous commit to avoid blocking clients. A crucial clarification: the acknowledgement confirms the replica has received and written the event to its relay log — it does not guarantee the replica has applied the transaction. This means semi‑sync significantly reduces the data loss window because the event is on disk on another server, but replicas may still lag in applying changes. A common misconception is to expect synchronous durability across replicas; semi‑sync is not the same as two‑phase commit. The takeaway is to tune timeout against expected network latency and replica load: too short a timeout causes frequent fallbacks and too long increases commit latency for clients.

keyIdea.title: Mechanism
keyIdea.text: Source waits for a receipt from a replica and uses a timeout to decide when to fall back to asynchronous mode.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Semi‑Sync Mechanism
Step sequence
1
Source commits and writes binlog
Commit is local; event is prepared for delivery.
2
Source sends to replicas
Replicas receive and write to relay log.
3
Replica sends acknowledgement
Acknowledgement confirms receipt, not application.
4
Source returns success or times out
If timeout occurs, fallback to asynchronous commit.
Notes and example
  • Receipt guarantees the event is stored on at least one replica disk, reducing loss risk.
  • If a replica is slow, network latency or heavy IO can cause source fallbacks; the timeout parameter controls sensitivity.
  • Misconception: semi‑sync is not equivalent to two‑phase commit; it only ensures receipt, not apply ordering across servers.
Key takeaway

Semi‑sync shifts the durability guarantee from local-only to 'received by at least one replica', narrowing the data loss window while keeping lower latency than full synchronous replication.

screens.title: Enabling semi‑synchronous on the source server
screens.narratorSegment: To enable semi‑synchronous replication on the source, you load the rpl_semi_sync_source plugin, enable it, and set a timeout that balances durability and latency. The canonical commands are INSTALL PLUGIN rpl_semi_sync_source SONAME 'mysql_semi_sync_source. so'; then SET GLOBAL rpl_semi_sync_source_enabled = ON; and SET GLOBAL rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout = 5000; where the timeout value is milliseconds. A practical example: you might set the timeout higher in geographically distributed setups where latency is larger, but remember that higher timeouts increase transaction commit latency if replicas are slow. For persistence add the same plugin and variables to my. cnf under [mysqld], for example plugin_load_add = 'mysql_semi_sync_source. so' and rpl_semi_sync_source_enabled = ON plus rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout = 5000. A common mistake is to install the plugin only temporarily with INSTALL PLUGIN and forget to add it to my. cnf, so settings are lost after a restart. Always test in a staging environment first and verify with SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Rpl_semi_sync%'; to confirm Rpl_semi_sync_source_status is ON and clients are connected. Enabling semi‑synchronous on the source server means install rpl_semi_sync_source, enable it, choose a sensible timeout, and persist settings in my.cnf to survive restarts.. In practical terms, commands, timeout settings, and persistence in my.cnf. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Source setup
keyIdea.text: Install rpl_semi_sync_source, enable it, choose a sensible timeout, and persist settings in my.cnf to survive restarts.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Enable semi‑sync on Source
Terminal: source commands
-- On the source server:
INSTALL PLUGIN rpl_semi_sync_source SONAME 'mysql_semi_sync_source.so';
SET GLOBAL rpl_semi_sync_source_enabled = ON;
SET GLOBAL rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout = 5000; -- milliseconds
Tip: Choose a timeout that fits your network; 5000ms is a common starting point.
Persisting in my.cnf
[mysqld]
plugin_load_add = 'mysql_semi_sync_source.so'
rpl_semi_sync_source_enabled = ON
rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout = 5000
If you only run INSTALL PLUGIN without adding to my.cnf, the plugin may not be available after a restart. Always restart and verify with SHOW STATUS.

screens.title: Enabling semi‑synchronous on the replica
screens.narratorSegment: On the replica you must install and enable the complementary plugin so it can participate as a semi‑synchronous client. The commands shown in the source are INSTALL PLUGIN rpl_semi_sync_replica SONAME 'mysql_semi_sync_replica. so'; followed by SET GLOBAL rpl_semi_sync_replica_enabled = ON;. After enabling, verify with SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Rpl_semi_sync%'; and confirm Rpl_semi_sync_replica_status reads ON. Once the replica connects, the source will report a client count in Rpl_semi_sync_source_clients. A concrete verification step: after enabling the plugin on both servers, run a test transaction and watch the source status counters. A common pitfall is enabling the plugin on the source but forgetting the replica side, so no acknowledgements are sent and the source falls back to asynchronous mode. To avoid this, add plugin_load_add = 'mysql_semi_sync_replica. so' and rpl_semi_sync_replica_enabled = ON to the replica's my. cnf so the setting is persistent. Remember that enabling the replica plugin alone does not change when the source commits; it only allows that replica to send receipt acknowledgments when it receives events. Enabling semi‑synchronous on the replica means install rpl_semi_sync_replica on the replica, enable it, and persist the plugin in my.cnf so it can send acknowledgements.. In practical terms, install the replica plugin and verify acknowledgement behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Terminal: replica commands
-- On the replica server:
INSTALL PLUGIN rpl_semi_sync_replica SONAME 'mysql_semi_sync_replica.so';

Confirm that the replica reports its semi‑sync status as ON and that the source sees a client count of at least one.

screens.title: Monitoring semi‑synchronous status
screens.narratorSegment: Monitoring is essential after you enable semi‑sync. The primary command is SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Rpl_semi_sync%'; which returns several counters and status flags. Important items include Rpl_semi_sync_source_status, which should show ON when semi‑sync is enabled on the source; Rpl_semi_sync_source_clients, indicating how many semi‑sync replicas have connected — after successful setup you should typically see a value of one if a single replica acknowledges; and Rpl_semi_sync_source_no_times_no_slaves, which counts how often the source fell back to asynchronous mode. A rising fallback counter signals either network problems, overloaded replicas, or an overly aggressive timeout. Concrete example: after enabling plugins on both servers and establishing a semi‑sync replica, you might see Rpl_semi_sync_source_clients = 1 and Rpl_semi_sync_source_status = ON. If you observe frequent fallbacks, increase rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout to give replicas more time to acknowledge, or investigate replica resource constraints. The takeaway is to use these counters to decide whether to tune timeout, optimize replicas, or accept occasional fallbacks for lower commit latency. Monitoring semi‑synchronous status means use show status like 'rpl_semi_sync%'; and respond to client counts and fallback counters to maintain desired durability-latency balance.. In practical terms, key metrics, expected values, and interpreting fallbacks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Monitoring semi‑sync
Sample status output
SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Rpl_semi_sync%';
-- sample rows:
Rpl_semi_sync_source_status | ON
Rpl_semi_sync_source_clients | 1
Rpl_semi_sync_source_no_times_no_slaves | 0
The expected clients value after a successful setup with a single semi‑sync replica is 1.
Interpretation
• Rpl_semi_sync_source_clients = 0 means no semi‑sync replicas acknowledged; check replica plugin and connectivity.
• Increasing Rpl_semi_sync_source_no_times_no_slaves indicates frequent fallbacks; consider raising timeout or checking replica load.
• Rpl_semi_sync_source_status = OFF means semi‑sync is not enabled on the source; verify plugin installation and my.cnf persistence.

screens.title: What is a Global Transaction Identifier (GTID)?
screens.narratorSegment: A Global Transaction Identifier, or GTID, is a unique identifier assigned to every transaction committed on a MySQL source. The format is source_uuid:transaction_id, where source_uuid identifies the originating server and transaction_id is a sequence number. GTIDs make replication transaction‑centric rather than file-and-position centric. Practically, this means that when a replica connects to a new source, it reports the set of GTIDs it has already processed. The source then determines which transactions the replica needs and sends only those. This eliminates the manual, error‑prone work of finding the correct binlog file and position after failover. A concrete example: instead of finding a binlog file name and position to resume replication, you set SOURCE_AUTO_POSITION=1 in CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO and let the GTID sets handle alignment. A common misconception is that GTIDs magically remove all human work; in practice you still must ensure transactional consistency, enable enforce_gtid_consistency, and set log_slave_updates where appropriate. The takeaway is that GTIDs greatly simplify failover and provisioning, but they require careful configuration to be reliable. In practical terms, format, purpose, and how gtids change replication management. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › GTID overview
GTID format
A GTID looks like: source_uuid:transaction_id Example: 3E11FA47-71CA-11E1-9E33-C80AA9429562:1
This pairing lets the system identify the exact transaction independent of file names or positions.
Benefits and caution
  • Simplifies failover and replica provisioning because replicas share executed GTID sets.
  • Requires enforce_gtid_consistency for safety and log_slave_updates if replicas may become sources.
  • Misconception: GTIDs remove all complexity — they reduce some manual steps but require configuration discipline.

screens.title: Enabling GTID mode safely
screens.narratorSegment: Enabling GTID-based replication should be done carefully, especially in existing environments. The core variables are gtid_mode and enforce_gtid_consistency. The gtid_mode has states OFF, OFF_PERMISSIVE, ON_PERMISSIVE, and ON; a phased approach OFF → OFF_PERMISSIVE → ON_PERMISSIVE → ON lets you convert an existing server without immediate enforcement that could break non-GTID-safe statements. enforce_gtid_consistency, when set to ON, prevents statements that are not GTID-safe from executing, enforcing safer transactional behavior. Also important is log_slave_updates which must be ON on a replica that might be promoted, so it can write replicated events to its own binary log. A typical my. cnf fragment for enabling GTIDs looks like: gtid_mode = ON, enforce_gtid_consistency = ON, log_slave_updates = ON. After a restart, verify with SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'gtid_mode'; and SHOW MASTER STATUS to confirm an Executed_Gtid_Set is available. A common mistake is setting gtid_mode=ON without enforce_gtid_consistency=ON, which can lead to replication errors if non‑GTID‑safe statements exist. Always test the phased upgrade path in a staging environment. Enabling GTID mode safely means use a phased gtid_mode change, enable enforce_gtid_consistency, and set log_slave_updates on replicas intended for promotion.. In practical terms, gtid_mode, enforce_gtid_consistency and log_slave_updates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Position‑based replication vs GTID-based replication
screens.narratorSegment: Traditional replication uses binary log file names and positions to tell a replica where to start reading events. This requires the DBA to find the correct file and numeric position after failover or when provisioning a new replica. With GTIDs the process becomes transaction-based: the replica reports the set of GTIDs it has processed and the source sends only the missing transactions. The key practical difference is in CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO: with position-based replication you must supply SOURCE_LOG_FILE and SOURCE_LOG_POS; with GTID-based replication you use SOURCE_AUTO_POSITION=1 and avoid file/position arguments. A concrete example: after importing a GTID-enabled dump on a new replica, you run CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO... SOURCE_AUTO_POSITION=1; START REPLICA; and the replica and source reconcile automatically. A frequent mistake is forgetting log_slave_updates on a replica that may become a source, which prevents that server from writing replicated transactions to its own binary log and complicates chained replication. The takeaway is GTIDs reduce manual coordination and human error during failover and provisioning, but require consistent configuration across servers. Position‑based replication vs GTID-based replication means gtids replace manual binlog file/position coordination with transaction sets and source_auto_position=1 for simpler failover and provisioning.. File/Position style
CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO SOURCE_HOST='source_ip', SOURCE_USER='repl_user', SOURCE_PASSWORD='pwd', SOURCE_LOG_FILE='mysql-bin.000123', SOURCE_LOG_POS=456789;
This requires accurate binlog coordinates which can be error prone during failover.
GTID style
CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO SOURCE_HOST='source_ip', SOURCE_USER='repl_user', SOURCE_PASSWORD='pwd', SOURCE_AUTO_POSITION=1; START REPLICA;
GTIDs let the replica and source negotiate which transactions are missing automatically.
Key takeaway

Prefer GTID-based provisioning when possible: it simplifies failover and reduces manual errors, but ensure consistency settings are enabled.

screens.title: Mental walkthrough: upgrade async to semi‑sync
screens.narratorSegment: This activity walks through the commands and expected verification outputs when converting an existing asynchronous setup to semi‑synchronous. Start on the source: check SHOW PLUGINS for rpl_semi_sync_source; if missing, run INSTALL PLUGIN rpl_semi_sync_source SONAME 'mysql_semi_sync_source. so'; then SET GLOBAL rpl_semi_sync_source_enabled = ON; and SET GLOBAL rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout = 10000 to be permissive during initial testing. On the replica, check SHOW PLUGINS for rpl_semi_sync_replica and install and enable it if necessary. Persist both plugin_load_add entries and enabled variables in each server’s my. cnf. After both sides are configured, verify with SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Rpl_semi_sync%';. A correct observable outcome is that the source shows Rpl_semi_sync_source_status = ON and Rpl_semi_sync_source_clients = 1. If instead the source frequently shows OFF or a rising Rpl_semi_sync_source_no_times_no_slaves counter, the likely cause is that acknowledgements are not arriving before the timeout — increase the timeout or troubleshoot replication connectivity and replica load. This mental lab helps you anticipate outputs and next steps without needing two physical servers immediately available. screens.title: Common mistakes and safeguards
screens.narratorSegment: When enabling semi‑sync or GTID there are recurring mistakes DBAs make that lead to outages or confusing replication errors. For semi‑sync, a frequent error is installing the plugin only on the source and not the replica; this leaves the source waiting for acknowledgements that never arrive, or immediately falling back. Another common pitfall is setting rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout too low for your network and replica load, causing frequent fallbacks and increased apparent inconsistency. For GTIDs, a major mistake is switching gtid_mode to ON without enforce_gtid_consistency, or failing to enable log_slave_updates on replicas that may become sources; this can result in replication errors when statements are not GTID-safe or when a promoted replica doesn’t have the binary log entries needed for downstream replicas. The practical safeguard is to use the phased gtid_mode transition for existing environments, to test plugin persistence in my. cnf, and to validate behavior in a staging cluster. The takeaway: treat these changes as operational upgrades — plan, test, and monitor — rather than flip switches in production without verification. Common mistakes and safeguards means test phased gtid enablement, persist plugin configuration, tune timeouts for environment, and enable log_slave_updates on promotable replicas.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Semi‑sync mistake
Forgetting to install/enable the replica plugin results in no acknowledgements and frequent fallbacks.
Timeout mistake
Setting rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout too low causes many fallbacks; set it to match network and replica performance.
GTID mistake
Enabling gtid_mode without enforce_gtid_consistency or forgetting log_slave_updates on replicas can break replication during failover.

Always validate plugin persistence across restarts, and run status commands after changes to confirm the topology behaves as expected.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we examine a practical gap in MySQL replication: the data loss window that can occur with asynchronous replication, and two techniques DBAs use to close that gap. First, we’ll define semi‑synchronous replication — a middle ground where the source waits for a receipt from at least one replica so committed transactions are at least received by another server. You’ll see how that acknowledgement changes durability guarantees and what it does not guarantee, namely immediate application on the replica. Second, we’ll introduce Global Transaction Identifiers, or GTIDs, which convert replication from file/position based tracking to transaction‑based tracking. I’ll show how GTIDs simplify failover and provisioning and which server settings are required. Throughout the lesson you’ll walk through the exact commands used to install and enable semi‑sync plugins on a source and a replica, the my. cnf fragments needed for persistence, and the verification commands such as SHOW STATUS and SHOW MASTER STATUS. By the end you will understand how semi‑sync reduces data loss risk, how GTIDs make failover deterministic, and what common configuration mistakes to avoid when enabling these features.

These four objectives map to practical DBA actions and conceptual understanding you need for robust replication. First, you will explain why asynchronous replication can lose committed transactions if the source fails before the binlog event reaches any replica. A concrete example is a high‑traffic write just committed on the primary that is still buffered for network transfer. Second, you will describe how semi‑synchronous replication reduces that risk by requiring a replica receipt before the source returns success, and you will explain the difference between receipt and application on the replica. Third, you will configure semi‑synchronous plugins on both source and replica, set rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout appropriately, and persist those settings in my. cnf so they survive restarts. Finally, you will define GTIDs, enable gtid_mode with enforce_gtid_consistency, and verify GTID status using SHOW MASTER STATUS and SHOW REPLICA STATUS. Each objective connects concept and command so you can both reason about durability and execute configuration in a controlled, testable way.

This second objectives slide focuses on verification and monitoring skills. You should be able to run the SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Rpl_semi_sync%'; command and interpret the important metrics such as Rpl_semi_sync_source_status, which indicates whether semi‑sync is enabled on the source, Rpl_semi_sync_source_clients, the count of connected semi‑sync replicas, and Rpl_semi_sync_source_no_times_no_slaves, a counter of fallbacks to asynchronous mode. You will also run SHOW MASTER STATUS and SHOW REPLICA STATUS to read Executed_Gtid_Set and Retrieved_Gtid_Set when GTIDs are enabled. These commands help you answer concrete operational questions: is semi‑sync active, are acknowledgements being received within timeout, and which GTIDs have been processed. Practically, we will cover interpreting a typical output where one semi‑sync replica is connected, what increasing fallback counters mean, and which configuration adjustments to try to reduce fallback frequency. Asynchronous replication trades immediate durability for low commit latency by not waiting for any replica confirmation before returning success to a client. To be precise: when the source commits a transaction and writes the event to its binary log, it hands off the event to the network and immediately returns success. If the source crashes before that event is received or written by any replica, the transaction is effectively lost — it exists in the source binary log or memory but not on any surviving server. A concrete example is a busy write-heavy system where a commit occurs and the network to the replicas is partitioned for a few seconds; if the primary fails during that partition, those last commits vanish. This is important because many production SLAs require zero or near-zero data loss. A common misconception is to equate 'committed' with 'durable across servers' in asynchronous setups. The correct mental model is that commit on the source guarantees local durability only. The takeaway is that understanding this window is the motivation for semi‑synchronous replication: we need a middle ground that reduces the chance of losing committed work while keeping latency acceptable. Reflect: in your environment, which transactions absolutely cannot be lost and are worth the extra latency to protect?

Semi‑synchronous replication offers a compromise: the source waits for at least one configured replica to acknowledge receipt of the binary log event before returning success to the client. Concretely, the sequence is: the source commits and writes the event to its binary log, sends the event to connected replicas, and waits for a receipt acknowledgement from one semi‑sync replica. If an acknowledgement arrives within rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout, the source returns success; if no acknowledgement arrives within the timeout, the source falls back to asynchronous commit to avoid blocking clients. A crucial clarification: the acknowledgement confirms the replica has received and written the event to its relay log — it does not guarantee the replica has applied the transaction. This means semi‑sync significantly reduces the data loss window because the event is on disk on another server, but replicas may still lag in applying changes. A common misconception is to expect synchronous durability across replicas; semi‑sync is not the same as two‑phase commit. The takeaway is to tune timeout against expected network latency and replica load: too short a timeout causes frequent fallbacks and too long increases commit latency for clients.

To enable semi‑synchronous replication on the source, you load the rpl_semi_sync_source plugin, enable it, and set a timeout that balances durability and latency. The canonical commands are INSTALL PLUGIN rpl_semi_sync_source SONAME 'mysql_semi_sync_source. so'; then SET GLOBAL rpl_semi_sync_source_enabled = ON; and SET GLOBAL rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout = 5000; where the timeout value is milliseconds. A practical example: you might set the timeout higher in geographically distributed setups where latency is larger, but remember that higher timeouts increase transaction commit latency if replicas are slow. For persistence add the same plugin and variables to my. cnf under [mysqld], for example plugin_load_add = 'mysql_semi_sync_source. so' and rpl_semi_sync_source_enabled = ON plus rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout = 5000. A common mistake is to install the plugin only temporarily with INSTALL PLUGIN and forget to add it to my. cnf, so settings are lost after a restart. Always test in a staging environment first and verify with SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Rpl_semi_sync%'; to confirm Rpl_semi_sync_source_status is ON and clients are connected. Enabling semi‑synchronous on the source server means install rpl_semi_sync_source, enable it, choose a sensible timeout, and persist settings in my.cnf to survive restarts.. The commands shown in the source are INSTALL PLUGIN rpl_semi_sync_replica SONAME 'mysql_semi_sync_replica. so'; followed by SET GLOBAL rpl_semi_sync_replica_enabled = ON;. A concrete verification step: after enabling the plugin on both servers, run a test transaction and watch the source status counters. Monitoring is essential after you enable semi‑sync. The primary command is SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Rpl_semi_sync%'; which returns several counters and status flags. Important items include Rpl_semi_sync_source_status, which should show ON when semi‑sync is enabled on the source; Rpl_semi_sync_source_clients, indicating how many semi‑sync replicas have connected — after successful setup you should typically see a value of one if a single replica acknowledges; and Rpl_semi_sync_source_no_times_no_slaves, which counts how often the source fell back to asynchronous mode. A rising fallback counter signals either network problems, overloaded replicas, or an overly aggressive timeout. Concrete example: after enabling plugins on both servers and establishing a semi‑sync replica, you might see Rpl_semi_sync_source_clients = 1 and Rpl_semi_sync_source_status = ON. If you observe frequent fallbacks, increase rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout to give replicas more time to acknowledge, or investigate replica resource constraints. The takeaway is to use these counters to decide whether to tune timeout, optimize replicas, or accept occasional fallbacks for lower commit latency. A Global Transaction Identifier, or GTID, is a unique identifier assigned to every transaction committed on a MySQL source. The format is source_uuid:transaction_id, where source_uuid identifies the originating server and transaction_id is a sequence number. GTIDs make replication transaction‑centric rather than file-and-position centric. Practically, this means that when a replica connects to a new source, it reports the set of GTIDs it has already processed. The source then determines which transactions the replica needs and sends only those. This eliminates the manual, error‑prone work of finding the correct binlog file and position after failover. A concrete example: instead of finding a binlog file name and position to resume replication, you set SOURCE_AUTO_POSITION=1 in CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO and let the GTID sets handle alignment. A common misconception is that GTIDs magically remove all human work; in practice you still must ensure transactional consistency, enable enforce_gtid_consistency, and set log_slave_updates where appropriate. The takeaway is that GTIDs greatly simplify failover and provisioning, but they require careful configuration to be reliable. Enabling GTID-based replication should be done carefully, especially in existing environments. The core variables are gtid_mode and enforce_gtid_consistency. The gtid_mode has states OFF, OFF_PERMISSIVE, ON_PERMISSIVE, and ON; a phased approach OFF → OFF_PERMISSIVE → ON_PERMISSIVE → ON lets you convert an existing server without immediate enforcement that could break non-GTID-safe statements. enforce_gtid_consistency, when set to ON, prevents statements that are not GTID-safe from executing, enforcing safer transactional behavior. Also important is log_slave_updates which must be ON on a replica that might be promoted, so it can write replicated events to its own binary log. A typical my. cnf fragment for enabling GTIDs looks like: gtid_mode = ON, enforce_gtid_consistency = ON, log_slave_updates = ON. After a restart, verify with SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'gtid_mode'; and SHOW MASTER STATUS to confirm an Executed_Gtid_Set is available. A common mistake is setting gtid_mode=ON without enforce_gtid_consistency=ON, which can lead to replication errors if non‑GTID‑safe statements exist. Always test the phased upgrade path in a staging environment. Enabling GTID mode safely means use a phased gtid_mode change, enable enforce_gtid_consistency, and set log_slave_updates on replicas intended for promotion.. Traditional replication uses binary log file names and positions to tell a replica where to start reading events. This requires the DBA to find the correct file and numeric position after failover or when provisioning a new replica. With GTIDs the process becomes transaction-based: the replica reports the set of GTIDs it has processed and the source sends only the missing transactions. The key practical difference is in CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO: with position-based replication you must supply SOURCE_LOG_FILE and SOURCE_LOG_POS; with GTID-based replication you use SOURCE_AUTO_POSITION=1 and avoid file/position arguments. A concrete example: after importing a GTID-enabled dump on a new replica, you run CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO... SOURCE_AUTO_POSITION=1; START REPLICA; and the replica and source reconcile automatically. A frequent mistake is forgetting log_slave_updates on a replica that may become a source, which prevents that server from writing replicated transactions to its own binary log and complicates chained replication. The takeaway is GTIDs reduce manual coordination and human error during failover and provisioning, but require consistent configuration across servers. This activity walks through the commands and expected verification outputs when converting an existing asynchronous setup to semi‑synchronous. Start on the source: check SHOW PLUGINS for rpl_semi_sync_source; if missing, run INSTALL PLUGIN rpl_semi_sync_source SONAME 'mysql_semi_sync_source. so'; then SET GLOBAL rpl_semi_sync_source_enabled = ON; and SET GLOBAL rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout = 10000 to be permissive during initial testing. On the replica, check SHOW PLUGINS for rpl_semi_sync_replica and install and enable it if necessary. Persist both plugin_load_add entries and enabled variables in each server’s my. cnf. After both sides are configured, verify with SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Rpl_semi_sync%';. A correct observable outcome is that the source shows Rpl_semi_sync_source_status = ON and Rpl_semi_sync_source_clients = 1. If instead the source frequently shows OFF or a rising Rpl_semi_sync_source_no_times_no_slaves counter, the likely cause is that acknowledgements are not arriving before the timeout — increase the timeout or troubleshoot replication connectivity and replica load. When enabling semi‑sync or GTID there are recurring mistakes DBAs make that lead to outages or confusing replication errors. For semi‑sync, a frequent error is installing the plugin only on the source and not the replica; this leaves the source waiting for acknowledgements that never arrive, or immediately falling back. Another common pitfall is setting rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout too low for your network and replica load, causing frequent fallbacks and increased apparent inconsistency. For GTIDs, a major mistake is switching gtid_mode to ON without enforce_gtid_consistency, or failing to enable log_slave_updates on replicas that may become sources; this can result in replication errors when statements are not GTID-safe or when a promoted replica doesn’t have the binary log entries needed for downstream replicas. The practical safeguard is to use the phased gtid_mode transition for existing environments, to test plugin persistence in my. cnf, and to validate behavior in a staging cluster. The takeaway: treat these changes as operational upgrades — plan, test, and monitor — rather than flip switches in production without verification. Let’s consolidate the essentials. Semi‑synchronous replication requires the source to wait for a receipt from at least one replica before returning success, which reduces the risk of losing committed transactions but does not guarantee the transaction has been applied on the replica. rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout controls how long the source waits before falling back to asynchronous commits. GTIDs uniquely identify each transaction as source_uuid:transaction_id and allow replication to be transaction-based rather than file/position-based. Enabling GTIDs requires careful configuration: use a phased gtid_mode transition if converting an existing system, set enforce_gtid_consistency to prevent unsafe statements, and enable log_slave_updates on replicas expected to be promotable. These practices combined make failover and replica provisioning far simpler and less error-prone. As you work with these settings, remember to test changes in staging and monitor the Rpl_semi_sync status counters and GTID sets for expected behavior.
